items.stem: Read Text A, an article from the island’s tourism board, ‘Open Arms, Open Island’: ‘Tourism is the lifeblood of our island. Last year more than 200,000 visitors brought in money that paid for a new clinic, resurfaced roads and kept our schools open. Over a third of islanders now work in hotels, restaurants, boat tours and craft shops, and young people no longer have to leave to find work. Visitors fall in love with our beaches, our food and our festivals, and many return year after year. A new cruise terminal would allow us to welcome twice as many guests. Some worry about crowds, but with good planning there is room for everyone. If we close our doors, others will open theirs, and our children will pay the price.’ Which of these points is made in Text A?
items.answer: visitors return and value culture
items.markingKey: Text A makes the point: visitors return and value culture. The other options come from the other text on tourism on a small island.

items.stem: In an article by a planetary scientist, ‘Why We Must Keep Looking Up’, the writer states: ‘countless young people choose to study science because of a rocket launch’ Explain why a reader might question this claim.
items.answer: ‘countless’ is vague and the link is not evidenced.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies the weakness (generalisation, lack of evidence, exaggeration, false choice); explains why it reduces the claim’s reliability; may suggest what evidence is needed.

items.stem: In an article by an animal-welfare campaigner, ‘Bigger Cages Are Still Cages’, the writer states: ‘Only a small proportion of species kept in zoos are part of programmes that return animals to the wild’ Explain why a reader might question this claim.
items.answer: No figure is given, so the claim is hard to check.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies the weakness (generalisation, lack of evidence, exaggeration, false choice); explains why it reduces the claim’s reliability; may suggest what evidence is needed.

items.stem: Read Text A, a speech by the director of a city zoo: ‘Good evening. Modern zoos are not the prisons of the past. Our animals live in large, carefully designed habitats, and every species has a care plan written by vets and behaviour experts. More importantly, zoos are arks. Our breeding programme has returned more than fifty endangered tortoises to the wild, and we fund conservation rangers in three countries. Every year, 400,000 visitors, half of them children, see living animals up close, and many tell us it is the moment they began to care about nature. A documentary cannot do that. Close the zoos, and we close the door on the next generation of conservationists.’ Identify 2 ideas the writer uses to support their view on the role of zoos today, and evaluate how convincing each is.
items.answer: Ideas: large designed habitats; expert care plans; breeding programmes return animals to the wild. Evaluation: ‘many tell us it is the moment they began to care about nature’ – anecdotal evidence from visitors chosen by the zoo; ‘Close the zoos, and we close the door on the next generation of conservationists.’ – a sweeping prediction presented as certain
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 per relevant idea; further marks for evaluation (quality of evidence, generalisation, bias, omission) rather than simple agreement.

items.stem: Read Text B, a blog post by a sixteen-year-old student, ‘Too Tired to Learn’: ‘I took a job in a café last September because everyone said it would look good on my CV. By November I was working fourteen hours a week, closing at ten on school nights because they were short-staffed and I didn’t feel I could say no. My grades dropped in every subject. I was too tired to concentrate, and I stopped going to football. Some of my friends cope fine, and the money was useful, but nobody warned me how hard it is to set limits when your manager is an adult and you are not. If you take a job, agree your hours in writing and protect your sleep. I wish I had.’ Identify 2 ideas the writer uses to support their view on teenagers having part-time jobs, and evaluate how convincing each is.
items.answer: Ideas: hours crept up (8 to 14); late closing on school nights; grades dropped; too tired. Evaluation: ‘My grades dropped in every subject.’ – a single personal case that may not represent others; ‘Some of my friends cope fine’ – acknowledges that her experience may not be typical, which weakens a general conclusion
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 per relevant idea; further marks for evaluation (quality of evidence, generalisation, bias, omission) rather than simple agreement.

items.stem: Read Text B, a letter from a market trader to the local newspaper: ‘The council’s cycle lanes will remove sixty parking spaces from Market Street. My customers are not students on bicycles; they are families buying a week’s vegetables and older people who cannot carry heavy bags on a bus. When the council closed Bridge Road for repairs last year, my takings fell by a third in a month. I am not against cycling, and cleaner air is welcome, but nobody asked the traders. A lane on the quieter parallel street would give cyclists a safe route without cutting off the market from the people who keep it alive.’ Identify 3 ideas the writer uses to support their view on building protected cycle lanes in a city centre, and evaluate how convincing each is.
items.answer: Ideas: loss of sixty parking spaces; customers need cars for heavy shopping; takings fell by a third during road closure; traders not consulted. Evaluation: ‘When the council closed Bridge Road for repairs last year, my takings fell by a third in a month.’ – one trader’s experience during a different situation (a full road closure); ‘My customers are not students on bicycles’ – a generalisation that may not reflect all customers
items.markingKey: Award up to 4 marks from: 1 per relevant idea; further marks for evaluation (quality of evidence, generalisation, bias, omission) rather than simple agreement.

items.stem: Read the two texts about spending public money on space exploration. Text A: ‘Space exploration is not a luxury; it is an investment. Satellites developed for space now forecast storms, guide farmers and connect remote villages to the internet. Research for space missions has helped improve water-purification methods and medical imaging. Studying other planets helps us understand climate change on our own. And exploration inspires: countless young people choose to study science because of a rocket launch or a photograph of Earth from space. The cost sounds enormous, but space agencies usually receive well under one per cent of national budgets. Abandoning space would save little and cost us our future.’ Text B: ‘While billions are spent sending robots to Mars, millions of people on Earth lack clean water. That is not a choice I can defend. Supporters of space programmes point to useful inventions, but many of those could have been developed more cheaply by funding the research directly. Private companies are now racing to launch rockets, so governments need not compete with them. If we want to inspire young people, let them see us solve the climate crisis, end hunger and rebuild crumbling schools. Mars will still be there in fifty years; the communities flooded by rising seas may not be.’ (a) Choose one claim from Text A and explain why it may be unreliable. (b) Choose one claim from Text B and explain why it may be unreliable.
items.answer: (a) ‘countless young people choose to study science because of a rocket launch’: ‘countless’ is vague and the link is not evidenced; ‘Abandoning space would save little and cost us our future.’: an exaggerated conclusion presented as fact (b) ‘many of those could have been developed more cheaply by funding the research directly’: a hypothetical claim with no evidence; ‘That is not a choice I can defend.’: presents a false choice: space spending versus clean water
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark claim; 2 marks evaluation [3] (b) 1 mark claim; 2 marks evaluation [3]

items.stem: Read the two texts about the role of zoos today. Text A: ‘Good evening. Modern zoos are not the prisons of the past. Our animals live in large, carefully designed habitats, and every species has a care plan written by vets and behaviour experts. More importantly, zoos are arks. Our breeding programme has returned more than fifty endangered tortoises to the wild, and we fund conservation rangers in three countries. Every year, 400,000 visitors, half of them children, see living animals up close, and many tell us it is the moment they began to care about nature. A documentary cannot do that. Close the zoos, and we close the door on the next generation of conservationists.’ Text B: ‘However well designed, an enclosure is a tiny fraction of an animal’s natural range. Elephants walk many kilometres a day in the wild; in captivity, many develop repetitive swaying and pacing, signs of stress that keepers call “stereotypic behaviour”. Only a small proportion of species kept in zoos are part of programmes that return animals to the wild; most are there because visitors like to see them. Conservation money is vital, but it could be raised and spent directly protecting habitats, where it does the most good. If zoos truly exist for conservation, they should keep only the species that need them, in sanctuaries designed around the animals rather than the visitors.’ (a) List three reasons Text A gives in support of its view on the role of zoos today. (b) List three concerns or arguments raised in Text B.
items.answer: (a) large designed habitats; expert care plans; breeding programmes return animals to the wild (b) enclosures far smaller than natural range; stress behaviours (swaying, pacing); few species in release programmes
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per reason [3] (b) 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: Directed writing task on replacing school textbooks with tablets: Write a speech for a debate at your school on the motion ‘Tablets should replace textbooks’. Evaluate the ideas in both texts and argue your own view. Without writing the full answer, write a paragraph-by-paragraph plan that shows which ideas from each text you will use and evaluate.

items.stem: Text A: ‘Space exploration is not a luxury; it is an investment. Satellites developed for space now forecast storms, guide farmers and connect remote villages to the internet. Research for space missions has helped improve water-purification methods and medical imaging. Studying other planets helps us understand climate change on our own. And exploration inspires: countless young people choose to study science because of a rocket launch or a photograph of Earth from space. The cost sounds enormous, but space agencies usually receive well under one per cent of national budgets. Abandoning space would save little and cost us our future.’ Text B: ‘While billions are spent sending robots to Mars, millions of people on Earth lack clean water. That is not a choice I can defend. Supporters of space programmes point to useful inventions, but many of those could have been developed more cheaply by funding the research directly. Private companies are now racing to launch rockets, so governments need not compete with them. If we want to inspire young people, let them see us solve the climate crisis, end hunger and rebuild crumbling schools. Mars will still be there in fifty years; the communities flooded by rising seas may not be.’ You are a resident who has followed the debate closely. Write an article for a science magazine for young people evaluating the arguments in both texts. In your article you should: consider who would be most affected by the decision; respond to the most emotive claims calmly and logically; explain which ideas you agree with and why. Base your answer on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: open in role (article to young readers of a science magazine); summarise the issue; evaluate Text A’s strongest points and weaknesses, then Text B’s; weigh them and give a clear, reasoned judgement of your own; close with a recommendation. Conventions: headline and possibly a strapline, engaging opening, clear angle, paragraphs developing the argument, effective conclusion.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Reading 4 marks, Writing 6 marks. Reading – top band (3–4): ideas from both texts selected, developed and critically evaluated; a clear, sustained judgement of your own; middle band (2): relevant ideas from both texts with some evaluation; lower band (1): ideas mostly repeated from the texts with little evaluation. Writing – top band (5–6): form, voice and register consistently suited to the audience and purpose; well structured and cohesive; precise, varied language; accurate; middle band (3–4): mostly appropriate form and register; clear structure; generally accurate; lower band (1–2): form or register insecure; loosely organised; errors affect clarity. Indicative reading content: Text A – satellites for weather, farming, internet; spin-offs (water purification, medical imaging); helps understand climate change; inspires young scientists; small share of national budgets. Text B – money could provide clean water; inventions could be funded directly; private companies can take over; inspiration from solving Earth’s problems; urgency of climate crisis. Evaluation – ‘countless’ is vague and the link is not evidenced; an exaggerated conclusion presented as fact; a hypothetical claim with no evidence; presents a false choice: space spending versus clean water. Writing: headline and possibly a strapline, engaging opening, clear angle, paragraphs developing the argument, effective conclusion; register suited to young readers of a science magazine.

items.stem: Text A: ‘Last year my class swapped printed textbooks for tablets, and I will never go back. A single tablet holds every book a student needs, so no more aching backs from overloaded bags. Digital texts are updated instantly, while our old geography books still described a country that changed its name a decade ago. Interactive diagrams and videos bring difficult ideas to life, and students who struggle can listen to texts read aloud. Of course, screens can distract, but that is a matter of teaching discipline, not a reason to stay in the past. Every student in my class now reads more. The future of learning is digital; schools that refuse to accept this are failing their students.’ Text B: ‘Before schools rush to replace books with tablets, they should look at the evidence. Several studies suggest that students remember more of what they read on paper than on screen, particularly for long, complex texts. Tablets are expensive to buy, insure and repair, and a broken screen can leave a student without any books at all. Many families cannot afford reliable internet at home, so “digital homework” widens the gap between rich and poor. Teachers also report that notifications and games compete constantly for attention. This is not an argument against technology, which has real value for research and accessibility. It is an argument for balance: keep printed books at the heart of learning and use tablets where they genuinely help.’ You are the parent of two teenagers. Write a letter to your headteacher, who is deciding whether to replace all textbooks with tablets next year. Evaluate the views in both texts and give your own recommendation. In your letter you should: identify and challenge any weak or one-sided evidence; compare the reliability of the two writers; consider who would be most affected by the decision. Base your answer on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: open in role (letter to your headteacher); summarise the issue; evaluate Text A’s strongest points and weaknesses, then Text B’s; weigh them and give a clear, reasoned judgement of your own; close with a recommendation. Conventions: appropriate greeting (Dear …), purpose stated in the opening, formal register, paragraphs, polite sign-off (Yours faithfully/sincerely).
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12: Reading 5 marks, Writing 7 marks. Reading – top band (4–5): ideas from both texts selected, developed and critically evaluated; a clear, sustained judgement of your own; middle band (2–3): relevant ideas from both texts with some evaluation; lower band (1): ideas mostly repeated from the texts with little evaluation. Writing – top band (5–7): form, voice and register consistently suited to the audience and purpose; well structured and cohesive; precise, varied language; accurate; middle band (3–4): mostly appropriate form and register; clear structure; generally accurate; lower band (1–2): form or register insecure; loosely organised; errors affect clarity. Indicative reading content: Text A – lighter bags/health; up-to-date content; interactive diagrams and videos; accessibility (texts read aloud); students read more. Text B – better recall on paper for long texts; cost of buying/insuring/repairing; broken screen = no books; internet access inequality; distraction from notifications; balance: use tablets where they help. Evaluation – an unsupported generalisation based on one class, with no evidence of how reading was measured; an exaggerated claim that presents a false choice between tablets and failure; dismisses a serious concern (distraction) without evidence; the studies are not named or quantified, so the reader cannot judge them; anecdotal reports; ‘constantly’ may exaggerate. Writing: appropriate greeting (Dear …), purpose stated in the opening, formal register, paragraphs, polite sign-off (Yours faithfully/sincerely); register suited to your headteacher.

items.stem: Text A: ‘Tourism is the lifeblood of our island. Last year more than 200,000 visitors brought in money that paid for a new clinic, resurfaced roads and kept our schools open. Over a third of islanders now work in hotels, restaurants, boat tours and craft shops, and young people no longer have to leave to find work. Visitors fall in love with our beaches, our food and our festivals, and many return year after year. A new cruise terminal would allow us to welcome twice as many guests. Some worry about crowds, but with good planning there is room for everyone. If we close our doors, others will open theirs, and our children will pay the price.’ Text B: ‘Sir, I have lived on this island for sixty years, and I no longer recognise it. In summer, cruise ships unload thousands of passengers into a harbour built for fishing boats. Rents have tripled as houses become holiday lets, and my granddaughter, a nurse, cannot afford to live in the village where she grew up. The coral reef our grandparents fished is bleached and broken by careless snorkellers and boat anchors. Yes, tourism brings money, but much of it flows to hotel companies based abroad. A second cruise terminal would turn our home into a theme park. We need fewer, better visitors who respect the island, not more of them. Yours faithfully, Mrs R. Fonseca’ You are a journalist who has read both texts. Write an article for a travel magazine evaluating the effects of tourism on the island, using ideas from both texts. Pay particular attention to the conventions of a article and to a voice and register suited to readers of a travel magazine. In your article you should: consider who would be most affected by the decision; respond to the most emotive claims calmly and logically; explain which ideas you agree with and why. Base your answer on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: open in role (article to readers of a travel magazine); summarise the issue; evaluate Text A’s strongest points and weaknesses, then Text B’s; weigh them and give a clear, reasoned judgement of your own; close with a recommendation. Text B – overcrowded harbour; rents tripled; locals priced out; damage to coral reef; profits go abroad; want fewer, better visitors. Evaluation – a vague reassurance that gives no detail of the planning; emotive scare tactic and false choice between expansion and closing doors; a striking figure with no source given; emotive hyperbole rather than evidence. Evaluation – a generalisation that ignores differences in workload and circumstances; second-hand, anecdotal evidence; a single personal case that may not represent others; acknowledges that her experience may not be typical, which weakens a general conclusion. Writing: headline and possibly a strapline, engaging opening, clear angle, paragraphs developing the argument, effective conclusion; register suited to readers of a teenage magazine.

items.stem: Read Text B, a letter from a market trader to the local newspaper: ‘The council’s cycle lanes will remove sixty parking spaces from Market Street. My customers are not students on bicycles; they are families buying a week’s vegetables and older people who cannot carry heavy bags on a bus. When the council closed Bridge Road for repairs last year, my takings fell by a third in a month. I am not against cycling, and cleaner air is welcome, but nobody asked the traders. A lane on the quieter parallel street would give cyclists a safe route without cutting off the market from the people who keep it alive.’ Which best describes the writer’s attitude to building protected cycle lanes in a city centre?

items.stem: In a press release from the city council, ‘Safer Streets for Everyone’, the writer states: ‘Businesses will benefit too, as people on bikes stop more often and shop locally’ Explain why a reader might question this claim.

items.stem: Text A on the role of zoos today argues: ‘breeding programmes return animals to the wild’. Text B argues: ‘enclosures far smaller than natural range’. Text A: ‘Good evening. Modern zoos are not the prisons of the past. Our animals live in large, carefully designed habitats, and every species has a care plan written by vets and behaviour experts. More importantly, zoos are arks. Our breeding programme has returned more than fifty endangered tortoises to the wild, and we fund conservation rangers in three countries. Every year, 400,000 visitors, half of them children, see living animals up close, and many tell us it is the moment they began to care about nature. A documentary cannot do that. Close the zoos, and we close the door on the next generation of conservationists.’ Text B: ‘However well designed, an enclosure is a tiny fraction of an animal’s natural range. Elephants walk many kilometres a day in the wild; in captivity, many develop repetitive swaying and pacing, signs of stress that keepers call “stereotypic behaviour”. Only a small proportion of species kept in zoos are part of programmes that return animals to the wild; most are there because visitors like to see them. Conservation money is vital, but it could be raised and spent directly protecting habitats, where it does the most good. If zoos truly exist for conservation, they should keep only the species that need them, in sanctuaries designed around the animals rather than the visitors.’ Which point do you find more convincing, and why? Refer to the evidence in both texts.
items.answer: Either view may be argued if supported: weigh the evidence offered for each (Text A is in favour of modern zoos; Text B is against keeping most animals in zoos). Weaknesses: anecdotal evidence from visitors chosen by the zoo; a sweeping prediction presented as certain; no figure is given, so the claim is hard to check; an assertion about motive with no evidence
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: clear judgement; evidence from both texts; evaluation of the quality of evidence; recognition of bias or perspective.

items.stem: Read the two texts about replacing school textbooks with tablets. Text A: ‘Last year my class swapped printed textbooks for tablets, and I will never go back. A single tablet holds every book a student needs, so no more aching backs from overloaded bags. Digital texts are updated instantly, while our old geography books still described a country that changed its name a decade ago. Interactive diagrams and videos bring difficult ideas to life, and students who struggle can listen to texts read aloud. Of course, screens can distract, but that is a matter of teaching discipline, not a reason to stay in the past. Every student in my class now reads more. The future of learning is digital; schools that refuse to accept this are failing their students.’ Text B: ‘Before schools rush to replace books with tablets, they should look at the evidence. Several studies suggest that students remember more of what they read on paper than on screen, particularly for long, complex texts. Tablets are expensive to buy, insure and repair, and a broken screen can leave a student without any books at all. Many families cannot afford reliable internet at home, so “digital homework” widens the gap between rich and poor. Teachers also report that notifications and games compete constantly for attention. This is not an argument against technology, which has real value for research and accessibility. It is an argument for balance: keep printed books at the heart of learning and use tablets where they genuinely help.’ (a) List three concerns or arguments raised in Text B. (b) Choose one claim from Text B and explain why it may be unreliable.
items.answer: (a) better recall on paper for long texts; cost of buying/insuring/repairing; broken screen = no books (b) ‘Several studies suggest that students remember more of what they read on paper’: the studies are not named or quantified, so the reader cannot judge them; ‘Teachers also report that notifications and games compete constantly for attention’: anecdotal reports; ‘constantly’ may exaggerate
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point [3] (b) 1 mark claim; 2 marks evaluation [3]

items.stem: Read the two texts about building protected cycle lanes in a city centre. Text A: ‘From next spring, the city will open twelve kilometres of protected cycle lanes linking the station, the university and the market. In cities that have built similar networks, cycling has often doubled within five years. Fewer cars mean cleaner air: road transport currently produces more than half of the city’s air pollution. The lanes will be separated from traffic by kerbs, making them safe enough for children and older riders. Businesses will benefit too, as people on bikes stop more often and shop locally. The scheme is funded by a national grant and will not raise local taxes.’ Text B: ‘The council’s cycle lanes will remove sixty parking spaces from Market Street. My customers are not students on bicycles; they are families buying a week’s vegetables and older people who cannot carry heavy bags on a bus. When the council closed Bridge Road for repairs last year, my takings fell by a third in a month. I am not against cycling, and cleaner air is welcome, but nobody asked the traders. A lane on the quieter parallel street would give cyclists a safe route without cutting off the market from the people who keep it alive.’ (a) Choose one claim from Text A and explain why it may be unreliable. (b) Choose one claim from Text B and explain why it may be unreliable.
items.answer: (a) ‘In cities that have built similar networks, cycling has often doubled within five years’: ‘often’ and unnamed cities make the evidence vague; ‘Businesses will benefit too, as people on bikes stop more often and shop locally’: a prediction stated as certainty with no local evidence (b) ‘When the council closed Bridge Road for repairs last year, my takings fell by a third in a month.’: one trader’s experience during a different situation (a full road closure); ‘My customers are not students on bicycles’: a generalisation that may not reflect all customers
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark claim; 2 marks evaluation [3] (b) 1 mark claim; 2 marks evaluation [3]

items.stem: Text A: ‘Space exploration is not a luxury; it is an investment. Satellites developed for space now forecast storms, guide farmers and connect remote villages to the internet. Research for space missions has helped improve water-purification methods and medical imaging. Studying other planets helps us understand climate change on our own. And exploration inspires: countless young people choose to study science because of a rocket launch or a photograph of Earth from space. The cost sounds enormous, but space agencies usually receive well under one per cent of national budgets. Abandoning space would save little and cost us our future.’ Text B: ‘While billions are spent sending robots to Mars, millions of people on Earth lack clean water. That is not a choice I can defend. Supporters of space programmes point to useful inventions, but many of those could have been developed more cheaply by funding the research directly. Private companies are now racing to launch rockets, so governments need not compete with them. If we want to inspire young people, let them see us solve the climate crisis, end hunger and rebuild crumbling schools. Mars will still be there in fifty years; the communities flooded by rising seas may not be.’ You are a member of a local youth group. Write an article for a science magazine for young people evaluating the arguments in both texts. In your article you should: compare the reliability of the two writers; evaluate the strongest argument in each text; suggest a practical compromise or solution. Base your answer on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: open in role (article to young readers of a science magazine); summarise the issue; evaluate Text A’s strongest points and weaknesses, then Text B’s; weigh them and give a clear, reasoned judgement of your own; close with a recommendation. Conventions: headline and possibly a strapline, engaging opening, clear angle, paragraphs developing the argument, effective conclusion.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Reading 4 marks, Writing 6 marks. Reading – top band (3–4): ideas from both texts selected, developed and critically evaluated; a clear, sustained judgement of your own; middle band (2): relevant ideas from both texts with some evaluation; lower band (1): ideas mostly repeated from the texts with little evaluation. Writing – top band (5–6): form, voice and register consistently suited to the audience and purpose; well structured and cohesive; precise, varied language; accurate; middle band (3–4): mostly appropriate form and register; clear structure; generally accurate; lower band (1–2): form or register insecure; loosely organised; errors affect clarity. Indicative reading content: Text A – satellites for weather, farming, internet; spin-offs (water purification, medical imaging); helps understand climate change; inspires young scientists; small share of national budgets. Text B – money could provide clean water; inventions could be funded directly; private companies can take over; inspiration from solving Earth’s problems; urgency of climate crisis. Evaluation – ‘countless’ is vague and the link is not evidenced; an exaggerated conclusion presented as fact; a hypothetical claim with no evidence; presents a false choice: space spending versus clean water. Writing: headline and possibly a strapline, engaging opening, clear angle, paragraphs developing the argument, effective conclusion; register suited to young readers of a science magazine.

items.stem: Read the two texts about tourism on a small island. Text A: ‘Tourism is the lifeblood of our island. Last year more than 200,000 visitors brought in money that paid for a new clinic, resurfaced roads and kept our schools open. Over a third of islanders now work in hotels, restaurants, boat tours and craft shops, and young people no longer have to leave to find work. Visitors fall in love with our beaches, our food and our festivals, and many return year after year. A new cruise terminal would allow us to welcome twice as many guests. Some worry about crowds, but with good planning there is room for everyone. If we close our doors, others will open theirs, and our children will pay the price.’ Text B: ‘Sir, I have lived on this island for sixty years, and I no longer recognise it. In summer, cruise ships unload thousands of passengers into a harbour built for fishing boats. Rents have tripled as houses become holiday lets, and my granddaughter, a nurse, cannot afford to live in the village where she grew up. The coral reef our grandparents fished is bleached and broken by careless snorkellers and boat anchors. Yes, tourism brings money, but much of it flows to hotel companies based abroad. A second cruise terminal would turn our home into a theme park. We need fewer, better visitors who respect the island, not more of them. Yours faithfully, Mrs R. Fonseca’ (a) List three reasons Text A gives in support of its view on tourism on a small island. (b) List three concerns or arguments raised in Text B.
items.answer: (a) income paid for clinic, roads, schools; jobs for over a third of islanders; young people can stay (b) overcrowded harbour; rents tripled; locals priced out; damage to coral reef
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per reason [3] (b) 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: Read the two texts about teenagers having part-time jobs. Text A: ‘A Saturday job teaches lessons no classroom can. You learn to arrive on time, deal politely with difficult customers and work as part of a team. Employers tell me that applicants with work experience stand out immediately. Earning your own money also teaches you its value: you think twice about spending forty hours” wages on a pair of trainers. Most students can easily manage eight hours a week without their studies suffering, and many find that a busy schedule actually makes them more organised. Start small, choose something you enjoy, and you will gain confidence that lasts a lifetime.’ Text B: ‘I took a job in a café last September because everyone said it would look good on my CV. By November I was working fourteen hours a week, closing at ten on school nights because they were short-staffed and I didn’t feel I could say no. My grades dropped in every subject. I was too tired to concentrate, and I stopped going to football. Some of my friends cope fine, and the money was useful, but nobody warned me how hard it is to set limits when your manager is an adult and you are not. If you take a job, agree your hours in writing and protect your sleep. I wish I had.’ (a) List three reasons Text A gives in support of its view on teenagers having part-time jobs. (b) Choose one claim from Text B and explain why it may be unreliable.
items.answer: (a) punctuality, customer skills, teamwork; employers value experience; learn the value of money (b) ‘My grades dropped in every subject.’: a single personal case that may not represent others; ‘Some of my friends cope fine’: acknowledges that her experience may not be typical, which weakens a general conclusion

items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: own judgement clear; reference to both texts; evaluation of evidence; logical justification; appropriate register.
